headline: Nvidia raises RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU pricing to $13,250 — 55% increase in a year
summary: Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU now costs $13,250, a 55% increase from its original $8,565 launch price a year ago. This surge is driven by global memory shortages and the ongoing AI boom.
details: Nvidia has quietly increased the price of its RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU to $13,250. This represents a staggering 55% increase over its original launch price of $8,565 just one year ago.

The price surge is attributed to the global memory shortage and the ongoing AI boom, affecting both gaming and workstation graphics cards. The RTX Pro 6000 series, including Workstation, Max-Q Workstation, and Server editions, was launched in March 2025.

While Nvidia lists the official MSRP at $13,250, actual retail prices can vary. For instance, the PNY RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell is listed at $11,359.99, and Newegg offers the standard edition for $12,099.99.

The data center-oriented Server Edition of the RTX Pro 6000 is listed on Newegg for an even steeper $14,999. Some listings may come from third-party sellers or be OEM units intended for system integrators.

Experts do not anticipate an improvement in graphics card pricing in the near future, with prices expected to continue climbing until the memory shortage subsides. Consumers are advised to compare prices across various retailers before making a purchase.

headline: Report by KPMG, a 'Big Four' firm, riddled with AI hallucinations and fake citations
summary: An investigation by GPTZero and the Financial Times revealed only 5 out of 45 citations in KPMG's AI report were accurate, with many claims about 'agentic AI' being entirely false.
details: KPMG, one of the world's 'Big Four' accounting firms, published a report in October titled "Total Experience: Redefining Excellence in the Age of Agentic AI." The report aimed to detail how companies are using AI to cater to customers' needs.

However, investigators for GPTZero, an AI content detection tool maker, found the report was full of AI hallucinations and included examples of agentic AIs that either did not exist or lacked the stated capabilities. These inaccuracies, including fake footnotes, were also verified by the Financial Times.

GPTZero's investigation revealed that only five out of 45 citations in the paper accurately pointed to real sources. A total of 28 citations paraphrased titles or added fake components to real sources, while 12 were too vaguely phrased to verify their existence, a phenomenon GPTZero termed "vibe citing."

Beyond the citation issues, approximately half of the claims in the paper were found to be fake or misattributed. GPTZero suggested these were "likely the result of an AI research tool over-complying with a request to find examples of 'agentic AI' in the wild."

For instance, KPMG claimed Emirates launched an AI chatbot named Sara that could alter flights, but Sara was a mobile assistant without AI booking capabilities. Similarly, UBS denied KPMG's claim of integrating agentic AI across its investment advisory, risk management, and compliance monitoring.

Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) also refuted KPMG's assertion that it uses AI agents to help passengers plan, book, and optimize trips based on preferences and real-time conditions. An SBB spokesperson confirmed the information was "not accurate."

Papers from highly trusted sources like KPMG are often cited in other research, raising concerns about a potential "poisoning the well of information" with second-hand AI hallucinations. KPMG has since pulled the paper and is reviewing the circumstances surrounding its publication.
